teaser: The strongest body in Russian painting, and it cannot think of a single thing to do.
review_notes:
Painted 1890 in Moscow in a room lent by the patron Savva Mamontov.
Vrubel's description of the Demon in a letter to his sister ('a spirit not so much evil as suffering and sorrowful, yet powerful and majestic'): paraphrased, not quoted.
Lermontov's poem 'Demon' and Vrubel's illustrations for the 1891 jubilee edition.
Size about 114 x 211 cm.
Work on church murals and mosaics in Kyiv (St Cyril's) and a study trip to Venice in the 1880s as source of the mosaic-like stroke.
Later Demons: Flying Demon (1899), Demon Downcast (1902); breakdown 1902, blind 1906, died 1910.
A tear on the cheek is often mentioned in descriptions; at this image resolution it cannot be confirmed, so the spot text only mentions the glistening eye.

lesson.text: Shoulders like boulders. Arms roped with muscle. A torso that fills a canvas more than two meters (about seven feet) wide. And this giant sits curled up with his fingers knotted together, staring at a sunset like a teenager nobody understands. The whole painting lives inside that contradiction: enormous power, nothing to use it on.

Mikhail Vrubel painted it in Moscow in 1890, in a room lent to him by a railway tycoon and art patron, Savva Mamontov. He was thirty-four, poor, and almost unknown. He had been trying to paint this figure for five years, destroying one attempt after another.

The figure comes from a poem every Russian schoolchild knew: Mikhail Lermontov's “Demon.” A fallen angel, banished from heaven, drifts over the Caucasus mountains, immortal and bored. He falls in love with a mortal princess, Tamara, and his kiss kills her. He ends as he began, alone.
Vrubel insisted his Demon was not a devil. He described him as a spirit more suffering and sorrowful than evil, and yet powerful and majestic. Think of a soul, not a monster.
How do you make a body look trapped when there are no walls and no chains? Vrubel does it with the edges of the canvas itself.
Follow how the figure is packed into the rectangle.

lines.label: The cut
lines.text: The top edge slices through the Demon's hair. If he stood up, he would go through the frame. The picture is simply too small for him, and you feel it as pressure.

lines.label: The knot
lines.text: Head, shoulder, hands and knees close into one compact lump. All that strength is folded in on itself, like a spring nobody releases.

lines.label: The gaze
lines.text: His eyes travel down and to the left, toward the yellow strip of sunset. He looks away from the flowers, away from us, at a light that is going out.

lesson.text: Squeezed, coiled, turned away. The pose alone tells you what the poem takes pages to say. But the oddest part of the painting is on the right, where the Demon is not looking.

Vrubel used a palette knife, a small flexible blade normally meant for mixing colors, to lay on much of the paint. Pressed flat, it leaves hard-edged slabs of color with sharp corners, which is why parts of this picture look chipped out of stone.

He had learned to think in slabs. In the 1880s he spent years in Kyiv restoring medieval church murals, and traveled to Venice to study mosaics, pictures built from small cubes of colored glass and stone. He carried the mosaic habit into oil paint.

lesson.title: Paint like cut stone
lesson.text: Move from the least solid thing in the picture to the most alive.

spots.title: Crystal flowers
spots.text: These are supposed to be blossoms. Painted in gray, white and pink shards, they look like quartz. Around the Demon even flowers turn mineral, beautiful and dead.

spots.title: The blue cloth
spots.text: His drapery breaks into flat blue facets, each a single stroke of the knife. No folds, no softness: it reads like the surface of a cut gem.

spots.title: The hands
spots.text: Fingers locked together, wrists bent hard. Of everything in the painting, this is where you sense the tension most. Strength with no outlet.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Young, almost girlish, under a storm of black hair, the eye glistening. Vrubel softens the brushwork here. The one tender passage is a face that will not turn to us.

lesson.text: Critics of the time found it ugly and wild. Yet within a few years younger Russian painters and poets were treating Vrubel as a prophet. Those broken planes of color, made in 1890, look startlingly like what the Cubists in Paris would arrive at nearly two decades later.

A year after this painting, Vrubel was hired to illustrate a luxury edition of Lermontov's works. His black and white drawings of the Demon were attacked in the press as crude and incomprehensible. Today they are counted among the finest book illustrations made in Russia.

The Demon never left him. He painted him flying in 1899, and in 1902 thrown down among mountain peaks, wings broken. He kept repainting that last face even after the canvas was hung in an exhibition. Weeks later he suffered a mental collapse. He went blind in 1906 and died in 1910.

Return to the first impression: a giant with nothing to do. Vrubel gave Russia an image of its own restless end of century, gifted, proud, and unsure where to put its strength. The sunset he watches is the last warm thing in the picture, and it is very small.

quiz.question: Which poem inspired the figure?
quiz.explanation: Vrubel's figure comes from Lermontov's poem about a banished angel.

quiz.question: How did Vrubel think of his Demon?
options: As the devil of church teaching
As a portrait of his patron
quiz.explanation: He described him as more suffering and sorrowful than evil.

quiz.question: What tool gives the painting its hard-edged, chipped look?
quiz.explanation: The flat blade leaves slabs of color with sharp corners.

quiz.question: What earlier experience shaped Vrubel's mosaic-like strokes?
options: Working on church murals in Kyiv and studying mosaics in Venice
quiz.explanation: Years with medieval murals and mosaics taught him to build images from small blocks.

quiz.question: How does the composition make the Demon seem trapped?
options: The top of the canvas cuts off his head and his body is folded tight
He is chained to a rock
quiz.explanation: The frame is too small for him, and his limbs close into a knot.

facts.text: The flowers beside the Demon are painted as soft, delicate petals.
facts.explanation: They are built from hard gray and pink shards and look like crystals.

facts.text: Vrubel went on to paint the Demon again, flying and then fallen.
facts.explanation: He painted a flying Demon in 1899 and a downcast one in 1902.

facts.text: The Demon looks straight out at the viewer.
facts.explanation: He looks away, down toward the sunset on the left.
